lead: A thin semiconductor strip carrying current in a magnetic field develops a small voltage across its width. The field pushes the moving charge carriers to one side, so one edge becomes slightly positive and the other slightly negative. This is the Hall effect, and the voltage it makes is proportional to the field. Hall sensors use it to measure magnetic flux density, to detect the position of a magnet, to count gear teeth, to clamp around a wire and read its current without breaking the circuit, and to find north in a phone compass. They are small, cheap, wear-free and work from DC to high frequency.
prereq: You need: sensitivity from Unit 1 (see static characteristics) and the idea of drift current in a semiconductor.

sections.h3: The Hall effect and the Hall voltage

blocks.text: Take a thin rectangular plate of n-type semiconductor. Send a current I along its length. Apply a magnetic field B perpendicular to the plate face. Each electron drifting with velocity v feels the Lorentz force F = qv × B, which pushes it sideways towards one edge.

Charge piles up on that edge until the electric field it creates pushes back with equal force. That sideways field, measured as a voltage between the two side contacts, is the Hall voltage VH. The build-up takes picoseconds, so the sensor responds almost instantly.

blocks.where: VH is the Hall voltage in volts; RH is the Hall coefficient in m³/C; I is the control current in amperes; B is the flux density in tesla; t is the plate thickness in metres.
n is the carrier density in carriers per m³; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge. For p-type material the sign of RH flips, so the Hall voltage reverses.

blocks.text: Two design facts follow. Thin plates give large VH because t is in the denominator. Low carrier density gives large RH. InSb with n around 2 × 10²² m⁻³ is about four to five times more sensitive than silicon with n around 10²³ m⁻³ at the same current, because its carrier density is lower. Its high electron mobility also keeps the plate resistance low, so a useful current needs only a small drive voltage and makes less noise. GaAs sits in between and drifts less with temperature.

The Hall coefficient is a material property of the plate. It is not the sensitivity of the sensor. Sensitivity is VH per tesla, S = RH I / t, and it also depends on the current you choose to push and on the thickness. Two plates of the same InSb, one 0.1 mm thick and one 0.3 mm thick, give outputs in a 3:1 ratio at the same current.

sections.h3: Driving the plate and reading the output

blocks.text: The plate can be driven by a constant current source or by a constant voltage. Current drive is standard: I is fixed, so VH = RH(T) I B / t changes only through the smaller drift of RH. The much larger drift caused by plate resistance changing the current is removed. Voltage drive makes the current fall as the plate heats, so the output drifts.

A practical sensor includes more than the plate. The Hall voltage is only a few millivolts, so a differential amplifier with high common-mode rejection sits beside it on the same chip. Many parts add a Schmitt comparator so the output is a clean digital switch.

items: Linear sensor: output is an analog voltage proportional to B, used for position and current measurement.
Threshold switch: output snaps high or low when B crosses a set level, used for proximity, gear-tooth counting and shaft speed.
Ratiometric output: the analog output scales with supply voltage, so the analog-to-digital converter should share that supply.

blocks.text: Signal-conditioning details belong to Unit 6 (see differential amplifiers). Two non-idealities always remain. Offset is the output with B = 0, caused by misalignment of the side contacts; it can be trimmed at manufacture or measured and subtracted. Temperature drift comes from RH and n changing with heat. A ratiometric part makes the output track the supply so a shared-supply ADC cancels supply error; a chopper-stabilised amplifier removes amplifier offset drift. The drift of RH itself needs temperature compensation or a matched pair.

A compass is a special case. The horizontal field of the earth is about 25 µT to 65 µT, a few hundred to a thousand times weaker than the field of a small magnet at a gear tooth (tens of millitesla). The compass part needs a high-sensitivity material and a low-noise amplifier, often with a flux concentrator and set/reset coils to cancel offset.
The figure shows the chain: current source, Hall plate in the field, differential amplifier, comparator.

examples.question: An InSb Hall plate has Hall coefficient RH = 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C and thickness t = 0.1 mm. A control current I = 10 mA flows while the plate sits in a flux density B = 0.2 T. (a) Find the Hall voltage VH. (b) Find the sensitivity in volts per tesla.
steps: Convert thickness to metres: t = 0.1 mm = 0.1 × 10⁻³ m = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Convert current to amperes: I = 10 mA = 10 × 10⁻³ A = 0.01 A.
Write the formula: VH = RH I B / t.
Multiply the numerator: 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.01 = 3.8 × 10⁻⁶; then 3.8 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.2 = 7.6 × 10⁻⁷ (units m³/C · A · T).
So VH = 7.6 mV. Part (b): sensitivity S = VH / B = 7.6 × 10⁻³ V / 0.2 T = 3.8 × 10⁻² V/T = 38 mV/T.
examples.answer: The Hall voltage is 7.6 mV, and the sensitivity is 38 mV per tesla at 10 mA control current.
examples.check:
RH = 3.8e-4
I = 10e-3
B = 0.2
t = 0.1e-3
VH = RH * I * B / t
print(VH)
print(VH / B)

code.code:
RH = 3.8e-4   # m^3/C
I = 10e-3     # A
B = 0.2       # T
t = 0.1e-3    # m
VH = RH * I * B / t
print("VH =", round(VH * 1000, 3), "mV")
print("S =", round(VH / B * 1000, 3), "mV/T")

traps: Do not confuse the Hall coefficient RH (m³/C, a material property) with the sensitivity in V/T: sensitivity is RH I / t and also depends on current and thickness.
Thickness must be in metres. Leaving 0.1 mm as 0.1 in the formula gives an answer 1000 times too small.
For p-type material the Hall coefficient is positive, so the Hall voltage polarity reverses compared with n-type at the same current and field. Examiners like this sign question.

The Hall voltage appears across the two side contacts, perpendicular to both the current and the field. On the wrong pair of edges the Hall component is zero, but you still read the resistive IR drop of the plate, which is usually much larger than VH.
A ratiometric sensor's output scales with supply voltage, so a wrong supply reads as a wrong field.

quiz.q: State the Hall effect in one sentence and give the formula for Hall voltage.
quiz.a: A current-carrying conductor in a transverse magnetic field develops a voltage across its width because the field pushes the moving carriers sideways. VH = RH I B / t.

quiz.q: Why is a constant-current drive preferred over constant-voltage drive for a Hall plate?
quiz.a: With current drive I is fixed, so VH = RH(T) I B / t changes only through the smaller drift of RH. Under voltage drive, plate resistance rises with temperature, lowers I, and adds a much larger drift.

quiz.q: A silicon Hall plate has RH = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C and t = 0.25 mm. Find VH at I = 5 mA and B = 0.5 T.
A gear with 40 teeth turns at 1800 rpm past a threshold Hall switch. What is the output pulse frequency?
quiz.a: Revolutions per second = 1800 / 60 = 30. One pulse per tooth per revolution, so f = 40 × 30 = 1200 pulses per second = 1.2 kHz.

quiz.q: A linear Hall sensor reads 2.500 V at B = 0 and 2.900 V at B = 100 mT, with a 5 V supply. An unknown field gives 2.650 V. Find the field and comment on the offset.
quiz.a: Sensitivity = (2.900 − 2.500) / 0.100 T = 4.0 V/T. Field = (2.650 − 2.500) / 4.0 = 0.0375 T = 37.5 mT. The 2.500 V quiescent output is the offset (half supply here); it must be subtracted before scaling, otherwise the reading is wrong by 625 mT if offset is ignored.

quiz.q: Why does an earth-field compass need a different sensor design from a gear-tooth detector?
quiz.a: The earth's horizontal field is only about 25 µT to 65 µT, roughly a thousandth of the field of a small magnet at a gear tooth (tens of millitesla). The compass needs a high-sensitivity material (large RH) with low plate resistance, a low-noise amplifier, a flux concentrator and set/reset offset cancellation, whereas the gear detector needs a fast threshold comparator and only cares about field changes of tens of millitesla.

beyond: Not for the exam. Integrated Hall sensors now come with on-chip coils that set and reset the magnetic layer, cancelling offset to a few microtesla, which is why a phone can act as a compass. Vertical Hall and tri-axis structures let one chip measure all three field components. In electric vehicles, coreless Hall current sensors measure pack currents of hundreds of amperes with galvanic isolation. Researchers are pushing Hall plates into wide-bandgap materials such as GaN and graphene for high-temperature and high-frequency work. Search for integrated Hall magnetic sensors, set/reset offset cancellation, and coreless current sensing.
